module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 699

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/699](https://www.erdosproblems.com/699)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos699

/-- Sylvester and Schur: for $1 \le i \le n/2$ there is a prime $p > i$ dividing `n.choose i`. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/AllenGrahamHart/FormalConjectures-Bench/blob/482dacc4d9335240f26218cdc62032da3100392b/formalizations/erdos699/Erdos699Formalization.lean#L7679"]
theorem sylvester_schur (n i : ℕ) (hi : 1 ≤ i) (hi_half : i ≤ n / 2) :
    ∃ p : ℕ, p.Prime ∧ i < p ∧ p ∣ Nat.choose n i := by
  sorry

/--
**Erdős Problem 699.** Is it true that for every $1 \le i < j \le n / 2$ there exists a prime
$p \ge i$ with $p \mid \gcd\big(\binom{n}{i}, \binom{n}{j}\big)$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_699 : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ n i j : ℕ,
      1 ≤ i →
      i < j →
      j ≤ n / 2 →
      ∃ p : ℕ, p.Prime ∧ i ≤ p ∧ p ∣ Nat.gcd (Nat.choose n i) (Nat.choose n j) := by
  sorry

/-- Erdős and Szekeres conjectured that, apart from a finite exceptional set of triples `(n, i, j)`,
one can always take `p > i` in the prime divisor statement. -/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_szekeres_strengthening : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∃ E : Finset (ℕ × ℕ × ℕ), ∀ n i j : ℕ,
      1 ≤ i →
      i < j →
      j ≤ n / 2 →
      (n, i, j) ∉ E →
      ∃ p : ℕ, p.Prime ∧ i < p ∧ p ∣ Nat.gcd (Nat.choose n i) (Nat.choose n j) := by
  sorry

end Erdos699

findings.description:
The Lean asks whether the set of all triples (n,i,j) with 1 ≤ i < j ≤ n/2 where no prime > i divides gcd(C(n,i),C(n,j)) is finite (`∃ E : Finset (ℕ × ℕ × ℕ), … (n,i,j) ∉ E → …`). The source conjectures that (5), P(C(n,i),C(n,j)) > i, 'holds except in a few special cases'. The original paper then describes those special cases as families rather than a finite list:
- i = 2 fails at special n, all powers of 2, by an explicit mechanism: n = 2^k with 2^k − 1 = pq, j ≡ 0 (mod p), j ≡ 1 (mod q). Examples are (16,2,6) and (2^11,2,713).
- For i = 3 there are 'a few scattered' counterexamples, and 'the numbers 3^α+1 have the best chance'.
- For i ≥ 4 there are 'only a few incidental' counterexamples.

The i = 2 mechanism keeps producing exceptions. I checked in Lean: 2^41 − 1 = 13367·164511353, with both factors proved prime by `norm_num`. Legendre valuations (`#eval`) give v_p = v_q = 0 in C(2^41, 285920731515), so gcd(C(2^41,2), C(2^41,285920731515)) is a pure power of 2. That makes (2^41, 2, 285920731515) an exception. The same computation gives further exceptions (2^67, 2, 23206563898901803639), (2^101, 2, 137177249633792241973877360183) and (2^137, 2, 16141961986503368055107762054812561012816). Their factors pass a Miller–Rabin test that is deterministic in this range. These go well beyond the known 16, 512 and 2048.

Standard heuristics predict infinitely many Mersenne numbers that are products of two primes of comparable size, and a positive share of these pass the digit test. So this family is very probably infinite. The Lean's 'finitely many exceptional triples, all i' reading is then very probably false, because of the very family the source singles out. The reading E–S appear to intend is left unstated: exceptions outside the i = 2 powers-of-2 family, or for i ≥ 3 / i ≥ 4, are finite. The literal reading of 'a few special cases' as 'finitely many' is defensible, hence 'questionable' rather than misformalization. The docstring's 'apart from a finite exceptional set of triples' is the same interpretation, not E–S's wording.
findings.source_evidence: Erdős–Szekeres, Austral. Math. Soc. Gaz. 5 (1978) 97–99 (scan: https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1978-46.pdf, which I read by decoding the page images). From p. 97–98: 'We also conjecture that P((n i),(n j)) > i (5) holds except in a few special cases. First of all we discuss some of the counterexamples to (5). (5) fails for i = 2 and some special values of n, all of which seem to be powers of 2. Assume n = 2^k to be of the form pq+1 where p,q are primes, e.g. 2^4 = 1+3·5, or 2^11 = 1+23·89 … The best chance for this to happen is if j … For instance … n = 16, … j = 6 … and when n = 2^11, p = 23, q = 89, j = 713 … The same method can of course be used if 2^k − 1 = u·v … There are a few scattered counterexamples for i = 3, e.g. ((10 3),(10 5)) … The numbers 3^α + 1 have the best chance. For i ≥ 4 there seem to be only a few incidental counterexamples to (5), we only know one such counterexample, namely ((28 5),(28 14)) = 2^3·3^3·5.' erdosproblems.com/699 (snapshot 2026-08-24): 'Erdős and Szekeres further conjectured that p≥i can be improved to p>i except in a few special cases. In particular this fails when i=2 and n being some particular powers of 2. They also found some counterexamples when i=3, but only one counterexample when i≥4'. zbMATH 0401.10003: '…P(…) ≥ i with equality holding only in a few special cases (several of which are given)'.
findings.suggested_fix:
If the intended conjecture is E–S's, restrict the finiteness claim so it leaves out the i = 2 powers-of-2 family. For example:
`theorem erdos_szekeres_strengthening : answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ E : Finset (ℕ × ℕ × ℕ), ∀ n i j : ℕ, 3 ≤ i → i < j → j ≤ n / 2 → (n, i, j) ∉ E → ∃ p : ℕ, p.Prime ∧ i < p ∧ p ∣ Nat.gcd (Nat.choose n i) (Nat.choose n j)`.
Alternatively, add the hypothesis `¬ (i = 2 ∧ ∃ k, n = 2 ^ k)`. Keep the current unrestricted statement as a separate variant if desired. The docstring should quote E–S ('holds except in a few special cases') and mention that the i = 2 exceptions (n = 2^k with 2^k − 1 = pq) are expected to be infinite.

reformulations.difference: The source says p > i holds 'except in a few special cases'. In E–S's terms, P(gcd) > i outside a small exceptional set. The Lean encodes the exceptional set through an arbitrary `E : Finset (ℕ × ℕ × ℕ)` of excluded triples and asks for a prime p > i dividing the gcd.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: (∃ E : Finset, ∀ n i j, 1 ≤ i → i < j → j ≤ n/2 → (n,i,j) ∉ E → ∃ p prime, i < p ∧ p ∣ gcd) holds exactly when the set of exceptional triples {(n,i,j) : 1 ≤ i < j ≤ n/2, no prime > i divides gcd} is finite. Forward: the exceptions lie inside E. Backward: take E to be the set's toFinset. Also P(gcd) > i ⟺ some prime > i divides gcd, since gcd ≥ 1. So the Lean is exactly 'finitely many exceptions'. Whether that is the right reading of 'a few special cases' is the separate questionable finding.

review.notes:
I checked all three declarations.

**`sylvester_schur`**
- It matches the source ('for any 1 ≤ i ≤ n/2 there exists some prime p > i which divides C(n,i)'; E–S: 'P(C(n,i)) > i for i ≤ n/2').
- Floor division is harmless: `i ≤ n / 2` in ℕ is the same as 2i ≤ n.
- `#eval` confirms it for n ≤ 80.

**`erdos_699`**
- It matches both erdosproblems.com/699 and E–S's Conjecture 1 ('For every 1 ≤ i < j ≤ n/2 we have P(C(n,i),C(n,j)) ≥ i'). The scan confirms '≥' in (4) and '>' in (5).
- The answer polarity is not inverted.
- The cases i = 1, 2 are automatic, since gcd > 1 always. The statement is non-degenerate, and no counterexample exists for n ≤ 80, consistent with the forum's search to 10^7.
- `answer(sorry)` shows as `True` in `#check`. That is the repository's default `answer` elaborator mode, not a defect.

**`erdos_szekeres_strengthening`**
- For n ≤ 80 the p > i exceptions are exactly (10,3,5), (16,2,6), (28,3,14), (28,5,14). This matches the forum data and E–S.
- The one issue I raise is how to read 'a few special cases': finitely many triples, or special families. The i = 2 family (n = 2^k with 2^k − 1 = pq) keeps producing exceptions at 2^41, 2^67, 2^101 and 2^137. The 2^41 case is fully certified in Lean: `norm_num` primality plus Legendre valuations. Heuristically this family is infinite, which would make the current finite-set statement false. The i = 3 family (both (3^α−1)/2 and (3^α+1)/4 prime) is heuristically finite. So restricting to i ≥ 3 looks like the version E–S would defend.

**Status**
All categories agree with the source. As of the 2026-08-24 snapshot, erdosproblems.com lists 699 as open ('FALSIFIABLE'), with partial results (true if j ≤ 3i/2 or n = 2j; finitely many n per fixed i < j). Bloom judged one claimed proof invalid in the forum. No status issues.
